title: Integrate marketing plans with business process

lessons.title: The marketing plan as part of the business
lessons.html:
Marketing is not just selling

Marketing is the process of finding out what customers need, producing it profitably and getting it to them at a price they will pay. On a farm, the marketing plan must link directly to the production plan, the financial plan and operations. A citrus grower who targets the EU export market must plan cultivars, spray programmes, certification and packhouse capacity years in advance. A broiler producer supplying a retailer must match placement of day-old chicks to the order schedule.

Contents of a marketing plan

  1. Situation analysis: market trends, competitors, SWOT.
  2. Target markets: who will buy, for example fresh produce markets (Johannesburg, Tshwane, Cape Town), retailers, processors, exporters, feedlots, auctions or direct sales.
  3. Objectives: measurable targets, e.g. sell 80% of lambs on contract at grade A2 within 12 months.
  4. Marketing mix (4 Ps): product, price, place (distribution), promotion.
  5. Budget and responsibilities.
  6. Monitoring: how results will be measured.

Market channels in SA agriculture

ChannelAdvantagesDrawbacks
Fresh produce market via agentOpen to all, daily price discoveryPrice volatility, commission
Contract with retailer or processorPrice and volume certaintyStrict specs, certification, penalties
Livestock auctionCompetitive bidding, quick cashTransport and commission
Direct to consumerHigher marginTime, marketing skill, compliance
ExportHigher prices for qualityPhytosanitary rules, currency risk

lessons.title: Linking marketing with production, finance and operations
lessons.html:
Integration in practice

A marketing plan fails if the rest of the business cannot deliver. Integration means every department plans from the same assumptions about volumes, quality, timing and price.

Production

Marketing tells production what to grow, how much, when and to what quality. If a retailer wants 2 tonnes of tomatoes weekly from May to August, production must stagger plantings, plan labour and protect against frost. Feedback flows the other way: if hail damages a block, marketing must tell buyers early and adjust promises.

Finance

The sales forecast becomes the income side of the cash flow budget. Price assumptions drive profitability calculations; marketing costs (packaging, transport, commission, promotion) are part of the expense budget. Contracts with long payment terms affect cash flow and may need production credit.

Operations and logistics

  • Packhouse and cold-chain capacity must match peak volumes.
  • Transport must deliver on time; late or warm deliveries are rejected.
  • Certification (for example GLOBALG.A.P. for exports, or retailer-specific audits) must be planned before harvest.

Human resources

Peak picking or slaughter periods need seasonal labour, training in quality standards and supervision. Plan recruitment early.

Tools for integration

  • A shared annual calendar showing planting, harvest, sales and cash flows.
  • Regular meetings between production, marketing and finance.
  • A single set of key figures such as volume forecast, price assumption and cost per unit.

Think of the business as a chain: a weak link anywhere, from seed to delivery, loses the sale.

lessons.title: Pricing, risk and monitoring the plan
lessons.html:
Making the plan work and measuring it

Pricing decisions

Know your cost of production per unit first. Price must cover variable costs in the short term and all costs in the long term. Compare cost with expected market prices from market information (e.g. fresh produce market statistics, auction reports, SAFEX prices for grain). Choose between selling at spot prices, forward contracts or fixed-price agreements according to the business's risk tolerance.

Managing market risk

  • Diversify buyers and channels so one lost customer does not sink the business.
  • Forward contracts and futures (for grains and oilseeds on the JSE commodity market) fix prices ahead of harvest.
  • Staggered sales spread price risk through the season.
  • Written contracts with clear specs, delivery terms and payment dates reduce disputes.
  • Check the creditworthiness of new buyers.

Monitoring and control

Track actual results against the plan every month.

MeasureExample target
Volume soldTonnes or head per channel
Average price receivedR/kg compared with market average
Quality% top grade, rejection rate
Marketing cost% of turnover
Customer retentionRepeat contracts renewed

When results deviate, find out why: was it price, quality, volume or timing? Then adjust either the marketing actions or the production and operations plans. Review the whole plan at least once a year.

Key points

  • The marketing plan must be built together with production, finance and operations plans.
  • Use the 4 Ps and clear, measurable objectives.
  • Know your cost per unit before setting price targets.
  • Manage market risk with diverse channels and contracts.
  • Monitor results monthly and adjust.
